messages.author: cb76670240837e52
messages.subject: Question regarding GGIR
parts:
I would like to thank you for developing the GGIR package. It is an excellent R package, and we are using it to analyze our accelerometer data for subject with autism and their relatives. We have few questions and were wondering if you could provide any suggestions.



1. We are analyzing 21 days activity recorded using GeneActive watch. Let’s take an example. On a particular day, a person fall asleep at 10pm (based on raw data), woke up around midnight, fall asleep again at 2:57 am and finally woke up around 7 am. The GGRI algorithm identified the period between 2:57 am and 7 am as the time of “sleep onset” and “wake time” respectively. In another example where the person fall asleep at 10:46 pm, woke up at 3:42 am, again fall asleep at around 6 and finally woke up around 8am, the algorithm identified the 10:46 pm and 3:42 am as the “time of sleep onset” and “wake” respectively. So it seems the algorithm is identifying the maximum sleep duration and choosing the sleep onset and wake accordingly. However, in the examples we mentioned, we think the whole duration should be taken into consideration. Could you please suggest how to do that? The two plots are shown in the attached PPT (slide2). Many of our subjects have fragmented sleep and we would like to capture and analyze  this trait.

2. We also noticed that if a person falls asleep in the morning and sleeps past noon, the sleep offset would end at 11:59 am, and the rest of the sleep period past noon would be excluded from that night's sleep. Is there a way to include sleep past noon as part of the total sleep time? Please see attached PPT (slide4).

 

3. In our analysis, we only used the raw GeneActive data and did not include data from sleep diary.  In the GGIR output,  we got the value of the variables "sleeplog_onset", "sleeplog_wake" etc. We were wondering how the algorithm calculates the sleeplog time without any sleep diary data?

 

4. We were wondering what is the difference between "acc_n_noc" obtained in part 4 and "Nblocks_nightsleep_pla" obtained in part 5. 


5. We were also wondering if the variable "Nblocks nightwak_and_IN30_pla" in part 5 provides the number of wake episodes during the sleep?

 

6. Does GGIR take into account daylight savings time?

messages.author: 8d92e34685fbc6bd
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Question regarding GGIR
parts:
Thanks Arpita, I believe we met on Skype and you are working in Pennsylvania. Nice to hear you are in the process of mastering GGIR.

1. Yes, the longest detected sleep period is used and I am aware that this is not ideal when people have fragmented sleep. Last year I listed the detection of multiple periods as a possible area for improvement. However, to do this I need some form of support, either someone paying me for my time to do the work or someone doing the work instead of me and making a pull request. This is not a trivial addition, because we would carefully have to think how this is incorporated in the GGIR results. So, for the moment I prefer to postpone this work until there is a well defined project with enough time to work on this.
2. If a sleep diary (sleep log) is available then GGIR can handle the so called 'daysleepers' who go to bed before noon and wake up after noon. If no sleep diary is available then this does not work yet. I can implement this based on the same conditions as the previous point.
3. I initially developed the code for a study that has sleeplogs. Later on when I started to facilitate studies without sleeplogs I kept on using the term to refer to estimated sleep window times. I am aware that this can be confusing and I also listed the improvement of variable names as a possible area of future work.
4. They are almost identical. Part 5 first identifies segments in the day and then splits it up in days. Part 2 and 4 first split the time series and then perform the analysis per day. The order of identifying days and performing the analysis may have a minor influence on the values.
5. No, the definition is more narrow: the number of wake episodes with acceleration level 'inactive'.
6. Yes, GGIR takes into account daylight saving time.

Kind regards,
Vincent

Dr. Vincent van Hees
Independent consultant
www.movementdata.nl
